transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (VP Eng - SummitTech), Maya Lopez (SRE), Ethan Cole (Platform)

[00:00] Alex Moreno: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda, we want to understand your current infra, use cases for LLMs, and whether Dedicated makes sense vs Hosted or Private. Priya will do a technical deep dive after a quick qual. 

[00:18] Daniel Park: Yep, thanks Alex. Quick context - SummitTech builds financial planning agents for enterprise clients, low latency interactive chat in our product, also some batch summarization jobs overnight. Security and data isolation are big for our regulated customers. 

[00:31] Maya Lopez: And we run in AWS, mostly in us-east-1, using EKS clusters. We try to keep data in our VPCs. We want predictable throughput and control over GPU capacity rather than pay-as-you-go spikes. 

[00:45] Alex Moreno: Great. High level question - are you looking to start with Hosted to move fast or jump to Dedicated/reserved? 

[00:52] Ethan Cole: We're evaluating both. Hosted is attractive for speed, but for committed throughput and cost predictability, Dedicated looks better. Also some clients require no multi-tenancy. 

[01:07] Priya Sinha: Understood. A couple of qualification items - what models are you planning to run (open or closed), typical sequence lengths, tokens per request, and peek QPS/burst patterns? 

[01:20] Daniel Park: We primarily plan to run a 13B open model variant initially for chat and occasionally a larger 70B for high-quality summarization. Typical interactive requests avg 256-512 tokens with a few outliers to 2k. Steady QPS is around 8-12 qps but we see bursts to 45-60 qps during payroll windows. 

[01:42] Priya Sinha: OK that helps. For Dedicated we size by concurrent inference capacity needed. With 13B quantized on A100-ish class GPUs you can get ~X tokens per second, but important tradeoffs are quantization, KV cache memory, and batching strategy.

[01:59] Maya Lopez: Can you clarify what you mean by burst capacity? We need guaranteed baseline and then ability to handle spikes without dropping requests. 

[02:08] Alex Moreno: Sure - Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools for your account, with configurable burst capacity that can use pooled excess capacity in a region or autoscaling with warm-up. There are two patterns: reserved-only with queued requests and predicted autoscale with pre-warmed instances. There's also the Dedicated+Burst addon for short spikes. 

[02:29] Ethan Cole: Any SLA differences between Dedicated and Hosted? 

[02:33] Alex Moreno: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets higher than Hosted, because you get isolation and capacity commitments. Hosted is multi-tenant with best-effort latency. We'll share the SLA doc in the follow-up. 

[02:45] Priya Sinha: On the technical side, we also provide KV/prefix caching to reduce end-to-end tokens for repeated context, continuous batching to improve GPU utilization, and model variant routing so lower-cost quantized variants can be used for lower-fidelity requests. 

[03:05] Daniel Park: That sounds helpful. Our main concern is data residency and key management - can you confirm KM integrations? KMS/HSM? 

[03:13] Alex Moreno: Yes, Dedicated and Private support KMS integration. For Private deployments we can integrate with customer HSMs. We'll attach the security checklist. 

[03:22] Maya Lopez: On networking - we need VPC peering or PrivateLink, and traffic must not traverse the public internet. How do you set that up? 

[03:30] Priya Sinha: For Dedicated we offer a private control plane and VPC connectivity options - traffic can stay in your VPC or go through PrivateLink. For Private on-prem you get a customer-managed control plane. We'll include network diagrams in the pack. 

[03:45] Ethan Cole: Can you give me a sense of cost differences? If we commit to Dedicated for predictable cost, what's the pricing structure? 

[03:52] Alex Moreno: Typically there's a base reserved capacity fee (monthly/annual) plus usage for overages. Pricing depends on GPU class and model footprint. For example, a 13B quantized workload on 8xA10 equivalent reserved nodes might be $Y per month; we'll send a tailored sizing/pricing sheet. 

[04:12] Priya Sinha: From an ops perspective, we also provide telemetry - token-level cost, latency breakdown by route, and per-model dashboards. That helps optimize batching and cache policies to reduce unit costs.

[04:28] Daniel Park: With bursts to ~60 qps, we worry about cold-starts and latency spikes if autoscaling is slow. What's warm-up time for new instances? 

[04:36] Priya Sinha: Warm-up depends on model and image; typical GPU instance warm start with model load can be 30-90s. To mitigate we do pre-warm pools and keep KV cache warm for canaries. Our recommended approach is a baseline of reserved nodes sized for 80-90% of expected steady qps, plus a small burst pool and fast fallback to compatible smaller variants if capacity constrained. 

[04:58] Maya Lopez: Are fallbacks automatic? We need deterministic behavior for SLAs. 

[05:03] Alex Moreno: You configure routing policies: fail-fast, queue, or fallback to a compatible quantized variant or region. For strict SLA customers we recommend cross-region redundancy + Dedicated reserve to avoid noisy neighbor impacts. 

[05:18] Ethan Cole: How about tenancy - is it single-tenant GPU allocation? 

[05:22] Priya Sinha: Dedicated is single-tenant at the pool level - your reserved GPUs are not shared with other customers. The control plane is multi-tenant but we provide audit logs and RBAC. Private goes further with a private control plane entirely in your network. 

[05:36] Daniel Park: We'd probably aim for Dedicated first, and then evaluate Private for our largest regulated clients. Our timeline for pilot is early Jan - want to see a POC with our sample workloads and latency targets. 

[05:47] Priya Sinha: Sounds good. For the POC we recommend a 2-week benchmark: we run sample traffic including interactive and batch, measure P95 latency, token cost, and tail latencies. We can test autoscale and burst behavior and share the runbook. 

[05:59] Maya Lopez: On compliance, do you have SOC 2 and ISO attestations and can you provide penetration test reports? 

[06:06] Alex Moreno: Yes we have SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001; we'll share certs and penetration test summary in the secure docs link. For Private deployments we can support additional audit requirements. 

[06:18] Daniel Park: One more - model rollouts. We need to be able to pin model versions per route and do canary rollouts. 

[06:25] Priya Sinha: Redwood supports per-route version pinning, canary A/B rollouts, and automatic fallback policies. The console gives visibility into token costs per version and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.

[06:40] Ethan Cole: Okay, some nitty gritty - do you support mixed-precision / int8 quantization and what performance hit should we expect on quality?

[06:48] Priya Sinha: Yes, we support int8 and lower-bit quantization. Quality tradeoffs depend on model; often int8 on 13B has negligible quality impact for chat, but for high-fidelity summarization we'd recommend int8+LLM finetuning or keeping 70B fp16. We'll include suggested quant profiles per model.

[07:09] Daniel Park: For the POC, can you run a comparison against our incumbent (we looked at Anthropic and Bedrock) on latency and cost? 

[07:17] Alex Moreno: Absolutely; we can include competitor baseline runs in the benchmark. Please share credentials or sample request traces if allowed. 

[07:26] Maya Lopez: Anything else we need to know about outage handling and graceful degradation? 

[07:31] Priya Sinha: We have routing fallbacks, model variant substitutes, and cross-region failover. Also, automatic queuing with backpressure headers we return to clients so your app can show graceful degraded UX. We'll share the error codes and recommended client behavior.

[07:50] Alex Moreno: Quick recap and next steps - action items: we'll send pricing and sizing, Priya will send the benchmark runbook and configs, and we'll set a POC kickoff for first week of Jan. Any blockers from you? 

[08:03] Daniel Park: Sounds good. I'll coordinate legal for the NDA and we'll review the security pack. Also need to confirm budget by 12/10. 

[08:12] Maya Lopez: I'll pull together our request trace and QPS distribution csv and share by 12/04. 

[08:20] Alex Moreno: Great thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links in email.

End of transcript.

Notes: Transcript contains some auto-caption errors (names/terms sometimes transcribed incorrectly, e.g., "KV cache" as "K V cash"), monologue truncations. References shared: dedicated-sizing.xlsx (link in follow-up), security-checklist.pdf (link), benchmark-runbook.md (link).
